new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed for this item and the compiler opened and quoted it, so there were no silent or not-opened works to spot-check. As a substitute I scanned every 'stress'/'accent' hit in the full thesis text (pp. 90, 173, 194, 195, 254, 255, 354, 382). The only stress mention not in the report is p.72 (PDF 90): the indefinite article be is 'phonologically independent, carrying its own pitch/stress', whereas the bound clitic -be 'does not carry any independent pitch/stress'; p.237 (PDF 255) adds 'despite the loss of stress, the construction is productive'. Both are consistent with the report and add nothing about stress placement. p.155 ('Longacre stresses that') is the verb; p.364 is…

new_statements.quote: In southeast New Guinea there are indications that tonal prosody may be present in some Goilalan and Binanderean languages and contrastive stress is found in the Koiarian and Baraic groups. The further southeast we go towards the 'tail' of New Guinea the less evidence there is of languages exhibiting tonal or pitch accent prosody or stress contrast. [...] Certain TNG languages require all syllables to be open, disallowing final CVC, e.g. Barai and other Koiarian languages, Korafe and other Binanderean languages, Kewa, Tauya and Yareban.

new_statements.relation_note: TNG-wide survey of tone/pitch accent/stress typology (after Donohue 1997, Ross 2005); southeast Papua largely lacks tone and pitch accent; Koiarian/Baraic = contrastive stress; Barai and other Koiarian languages have open syllables only (which the Namiae NT text contradicts for Namiae: 36% of word types consonant-final).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level, secondhand: languages of the Koiarian family (incl. the Baraic branch that contains Barai-Namiae) have contrastive (lexical) stress and lack tone/pitch accent; no positional rule; nothing said about Namiae individually.
new_statements.identity_note: Family survey chapter. p.56 sect 2.3.1.20 lists 'Barai-Namiae: Barai [bbb] 800; grammar: Olson 1981 / Namiae [nvm] 1,200; new testament: Ewande et al. 2004' -- Namiae is named but has no description; the prosody sentence on p.88 is a group-level generalisation over 'the Koiarian and Baraic groups' (Namiae belongs to Baraic > Barai-Namiae), drawn secondhand from Dutton 2010 / Olson, not from Namiae data. So it bears on nami1258 only as a member of the group.

sources.citation: Olson, Mike. 1975. Barai grammar highlights. In T.E. Dutton (ed.), Studies in languages of Central and South-East Papua, 471-512. Pacific Linguistics C-29. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-C29.471
sources.note: BARAI (Birari dialect, upper Bariji; note 1 p.511), not Namiae. p.474: 'Stress is contrastive on the word level and is defined as a combination of pitch, and either length or intensity. There are two contrastive pitch levels, high and low. To mark stress, high pitch combines with increased intensity and low pitch combines with length. Note the four possible combinations on the following two syllable words: íko before, ikò sew, ìre food, and iré stand.' 'Secondary stress has been observed in the longer words but needs further analysis.'

sources.citation: Ewande, Rosemary, Clement Java & Winnyfaith Nai (trs.). 2004. Godon Vuak Ma Ijin: The New Testament in the Namiai language of Papua New Guinea. Orlando: Wycliffe Bible Translators. Digital text edition 'nvm' at eBible.org (© 2004 Wycliffe).
sources.note: No phonology content (scripture text, no front-matter orthography note in the digital edition). Checked as primary data: 277,448 tokens, 9,465 word types, zero accented/tone-marked letters (so the Barai OPD convention 'tone marked on only few words' is not applied in Namiae orthography); 3,450 of 9,465 word types are consonant-final (izeg, oijon, keof, unam, tavan, besum), i.e. closed syllables are common, unlike the V/CV-only syllable canon reported for Birarie Barai -- Namiae has reduced/lost final vowels, a difference that bears on prosody and cautions against transferring Barai statements…
